title: Rip Van Winkle

teacherSummary.text: Good-natured, idle Rip Van Winkle wanders into the Catskill Mountains to escape his scolding wife, meets strange men in old Dutch dress playing ninepins, drinks their liquor, and falls asleep. He wakes twenty years later, bearded and stiff. In the village, King George's portrait has become George Washington, his wife is dead, and the Revolution has happened. He settles into old age telling his story.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Rip Van Winkle,” how does Irving show waking into a changed nation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Rip Van Winkle, how does Irving develop the idea of waking into a changed nation? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Rip Van Winkle develops the idea of waking into a changed nation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Rip Van Winkle (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of waking into a changed nation. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Rip Van Winkle suggests about waking into a changed nation. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's setting and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Washington Irving uses setting in Rip Van Winkle to complicate the reader's understanding of waking into a changed nation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Rip Van Winkle within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of waking into a changed nation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Rip Van Winkle alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of waking into a changed nation follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Rip Van Winkle and its treatment of waking into a changed nation. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's setting and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Rip Van Winkle as evidence for a larger claim about waking into a changed nation in Rip Van Winkle. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Rip Van Winkle as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of waking into a changed nation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Rip Van Winkle.

satQuestions.passage: On waking, he found himself on the green knoll whence he had first seen the old man of the glen. He rubbed his eyes--it was a bright sunny morning. The birds were hopping and twittering among the bushes, and the eagle was wheeling aloft, and breasting the pure mountain breeze. "Surely," thought Rip, "I have not slept here all night." He recalled the occurrences before he fell asleep. The strange man with the keg of liquor--the mountain ravine--the wild retreat among the rocks--the woe-begone party at ninepins--the flagon--"Oh! that flagon! that wicked flagon!" thought Rip--"what excuse shall I make to Dame Van Winkle?"

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
